parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man orders a birthday cake from a bakery.
script: Good afternoon, Sugar and Spice Bakery, Rosa speaking.
Hi. I'd like to order a birthday cake for my daughter.
Lovely. Can I take your name?
Callum Reid. R, E, I, D.
And how old will your daughter be?
Most kids want chocolate, but she doesn't like it, so lemon, please.
Lemon is very popular. Do you have a particular shape in mind?
She loves butterflies, so could you make it in the shape of a butterfly?
Of course. How many people does it need to serve?
About twenty-five. It's quite a big party.
Would you like her name on it?
Yes, please, in purple icing. That's her favourite colour.
Are there any allergies we should know about?
Yes, one of her friends can't eat eggs, so could it be made without eggs?
That's no problem. We do egg-free cakes regularly. When would you like to collect it?
That's fine. The total price is fifty-five pounds, and we ask for a deposit of twenty pounds when you order.
Can I pay the deposit by card over the phone?

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A supervisor gives new staff an introduction to working at a theme park.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Adventure Valley. I'm Phil, one of the operations supervisors, and I'll be giving you your introduction today.

You'll hear a lot about customer service and keeping queues moving. Those things matter, but our number one priority is always safety. If you ever have to choose between speed and safety, choose safety.
Your uniform will be provided, but the one thing you must never forget is your name badge. It must be worn at all times when you're working.
On a full shift, you'll have a thirty-minute lunch break, plus two shorter breaks of ten minutes each.
If you find a lost child, stay calm, don't leave them alone, and take them to Guest Services near the main gate. Don't call the police yourself; Guest Services will handle that if necessary.
Now, let me explain what you'll be doing in some of the different areas. At Splash River, our water ride, staff hand out plastic ponchos to visitors who want to stay dry.
At the Dragon Coaster, your main job is to check the height of children before they join the queue. There's a strict minimum height.
At the main gate, staff stamp visitors' hands, so they can leave the park and come back in later.
On the Ghost Train, visitors aren't allowed to take bags on the ride, so staff collect them and look after them until the end.
At the carousel, staff help parents with pushchairs, as it can get very crowded.
And in the food court, the main job is clearing tables, so that there's always somewhere for people to sit.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two economics students, Ines and Rory, discuss their study of a local street market.
script: Ines, let's go through our findings on Kingsgate Market before we start writing.
OK. Remember, we chose it because the council is considering closing it, so it's very topical.
Right. Our main method was interviewing the stallholders, and we also counted visitors on three different days.
And the stallholders all said the same thing. Their biggest problem is rising rent. The council has increased it three times in five years.
Yes. What surprised me was the visitors. I expected mainly older people, but there were far more young customers than I'd thought, especially at the food stalls.
That's a really important point for our report. So what should we recommend?
I think the market should open in the evenings, at least on Fridays. That's when young people have time.
Agreed. Let's check our key figures. The market was founded in 1890.
And today there are sixty-four stalls, compared with a hundred and twenty in the 1990s.
Average daily visitors: about three thousand five hundred.
The most common product sold is vegetables, followed by clothes.
And the council's proposal is to build flats on the site.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of timekeeping.
script: Good morning. Today's topic is the history of timekeeping: how humans learned to measure time with increasing accuracy.
The earliest devices were sundials, used in ancient Egypt, which told the time from the position of a shadow. Their obvious limitation was that they didn't work at night or on cloudy days.

Water clocks solved this problem. They measured time by the steady flow of water from one container to another, and they were widely used in Egypt, Greece and China. One of the most impressive was built in China by Su Song in 1088: a huge clock tower driven by a water wheel.

Mechanical clocks appeared in Europe in the thirteenth century, mainly in monasteries, where monks needed to know when to pray. These early clocks were very inaccurate, often gaining or losing around fifteen minutes a day.
A major breakthrough came in 1656, when the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens invented the pendulum clock. Its accuracy improved to around fifteen seconds a day.

Accurate time was also essential at sea, because sailors needed it to calculate their longitude. In the eighteenth century, the English carpenter John Harrison built a marine chronometer that kept accurate time even on a moving ship.

Railways created a new need for standard time. Before trains, each town kept its own local time. In Britain, railway companies adopted a single national time, and it was made legal for the whole country in 1880.

In the twentieth century, quartz clocks appeared. They use crystals that vibrate at a precise rate when electricity passes through them. Today the most accurate clocks of all are atomic clocks, which measure the vibrations of caesium atoms. Systems such as GPS depend on atomic clocks carried on satellites.

passages.title: The Tasmanian Tiger
paragraphs: The thylacine, better known as the Tasmanian tiger, was one of the most remarkable animals of modern times. Despite its name and its dog-like appearance, it was neither a tiger nor a relative of wolves. It was a marsupial, more closely related to kangaroos than to dogs, and its resemblance to wolves is an example of how unrelated animals can evolve similar shapes when they live similar lives. Its common name came from the dark stripes across its back. Unusually, both males and females had a pouch.

Thylacines once lived across mainland Australia and New Guinea, but they disappeared from the mainland around 3,000 years ago, long before Europeans arrived. Scientists believe that competition from dingoes, wild dogs introduced by people, and changes in human hunting may have been responsible. By the time of European settlement, thylacines survived only on the island of Tasmania.

There, they came into conflict with sheep farmers, who blamed them for killing their animals, although many historians now believe that the threat was greatly exaggerated. Between 1888 and 1909, the Tasmanian government paid a bounty for every thylacine killed, and a total of 2,184 bounties were paid. Hunting, combined with habitat loss and disease, caused the population to collapse.

The last known thylacine died in Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936. Just two months earlier, the species had been given legal protection, but it was too late. Film taken of the animal in its final years is often shown in documentaries. The thylacine was officially declared extinct in 1982.

Even so, many people refuse to believe that the animal has gone. Hundreds of sightings have been reported in Tasmania and on the mainland since 1936, and some enthusiasts continue to search remote forests with cameras. None of these sightings has been confirmed with clear evidence.

In 2022, scientists at the University of Melbourne announced a partnership with a biotechnology company that aims to bring the thylacine back. The plan involves editing the genes of a living relative, a small marsupial called the dunnart, to make it more like a thylacine. Many scientists are sceptical, arguing that such an animal would not truly be a thylacine and that the money would be better spent protecting species that still exist.

passages.title: Smart Cities
paragraphs: Around the world, cities are installing networks of sensors, cameras and connected devices that collect data on everything from traffic to air quality. Supporters call these 'smart cities', and argue that technology can make urban life more efficient, sustainable and pleasant. One of the most ambitious examples is Songdo in South Korea, a new city built from scratch on land reclaimed from the sea, where systems for transport, energy and waste were designed to be digitally connected from the start.

Transport has been an early focus. In Barcelona, sensors embedded in parking spaces tell drivers where spaces are free, reducing the time they spend circling the streets, and smart street lights dim automatically when no one is nearby. Singapore introduced an electronic road pricing system in 1998, which charges drivers for using busy roads at peak times, with prices adjusted according to traffic levels.

Technology can also help cities manage resources. Sensors in water pipes can detect leaks quickly, reducing the large amounts of treated water that many cities lose before it reaches homes. Smart grids, which use data to balance electricity supply and demand, make it easier to rely on renewable sources such as solar and wind power.

However, the collection of so much data raises serious concerns about privacy. In Toronto, a plan by Sidewalk Labs, a company linked to Google, to build a high-tech neighbourhood on the waterfront was abandoned in 2020. The company officially cited economic uncertainty, but the project had faced strong criticism from residents and privacy campaigners, who questioned who would own and control the data collected about people's movements.

There are also concerns about fairness. Services that depend on smartphones and internet access may exclude people who cannot afford them or do not know how to use them, particularly elderly and low-income residents. This gap between those who have access to digital technology and those who do not is often called the digital divide.

Some of the earliest smart cities have also been criticised for lacking life. Visitors to Songdo have described it as efficient but strangely empty, with fewer residents than planned. The lesson, many urban planners now argue, is that technology should be a tool to meet residents' needs, rather than an end in itself. The smartest cities, in this view, are those that ask their citizens what problems they want solved.

passages.title: Insects on the Menu
paragraphs: For most people in Europe and North America, the idea of eating insects provokes disgust. Yet according to a report by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, around two billion people around the world already include insects in their diets. In parts of Thailand, Mexico and Central Africa, crickets, grasshoppers and caterpillars are popular foods, often regarded as delicacies.

The environmental case for eating insects is strong. Because insects are cold-blooded, they do not use energy to keep warm, and they convert feed into body mass far more efficiently than cattle, pigs or chickens. Insect farming also produces much lower greenhouse gas emissions and requires far less land and water than conventional livestock. As the global population grows, supporters argue, insects could provide a sustainable source of protein.

Nutritionally, insects compare well with meat. Many species are rich in protein, as well as in iron, zinc and vitamin B12. In my view, the claim that insects are a poor substitute for meat is simply not supported by the evidence.

The main obstacle is cultural. But attitudes to food can change surprisingly quickly. Sushi, made with raw fish, was considered strange and unappealing by many Westerners in the 1970s; today it is sold in supermarkets across Europe and North America. Companies selling insect foods have found that consumers are much more willing to try them when they are processed into a powder and added to bread, pasta or snack bars, so that the insects themselves are not visible. In 2021, the European Union approved dried mealworms as safe for human consumption, opening the way for wider sales.

There are, however, reasons for caution. People who are allergic to shellfish may also react to some insects, since they contain similar proteins. Insect products are currently more expensive than many meat products, because production is still small. And the environmental benefits depend heavily on what the insects are fed: if they are fed on grain that could have been eaten by humans, much of the advantage is lost. The ideal is to raise them on food waste or agricultural by-products.

I believe insects should be seen as a useful addition to our food system rather than a miracle solution. One of their most valuable uses may not be on our plates at all, but as feed for farmed fish and chickens, replacing soy and fishmeal whose production causes deforestation and overfishing. Whether or not Westerners learn to love crickets, insects are likely to play a growing role in feeding the world.

task1.text: The line graph below shows sales, in millions of copies, of printed books, e-books and audiobooks in one country between 2012 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

chart.title: Book sales by format (millions of copies)

model: The line graph shows how many printed books, e-books and audiobooks were sold in one country between 2012 and 2024.

Overall, printed books remained by far the most popular format throughout the period, despite some fluctuation. E-book sales rose and then fell back, while audiobooks grew steadily and had overtaken e-books by the end of the period.

In 2012, 180 million printed books were sold, compared with 40 million e-books and just 5 million audiobooks. Over the next six years, sales of printed books declined to 160 million, while e-book sales increased to a peak of 60 million in 2015 before dropping slightly to 55 million in 2018.

After 2018, the trends changed. Printed book sales recovered to 175 million in 2021 and remained fairly stable at 170 million in 2024. E-book sales, by contrast, continued to fall, to 42 million. Meanwhile, audiobook sales grew rapidly, almost doubling between 2018 and 2021 and reaching 45 million in 2024, slightly more than e-books.

task2.text: Some people believe that employers should not be allowed to contact employees by phone or email outside working hours. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: Smartphones have made it possible for employers to reach their staff at any time of day or night. In response, some countries, such as France, have introduced a 'right to disconnect', allowing employees to ignore work messages outside their working hours. I largely agree that employers should not contact staff outside working hours, except in genuine emergencies.

The main argument for such a rule is the protection of employees' health and private lives. When workers feel they must always be available, they find it difficult to relax, and the boundary between work and home disappears. This can lead to stress, poor sleep and burnout, which in turn reduce productivity. Employees also have a right to spend time with their families and pursue their own interests without being interrupted by their manager.

On the other hand, a complete ban could be impractical. In some jobs, such as healthcare or IT support, unexpected problems must be dealt with immediately. In international companies, colleagues work in different time zones, so one person's evening is another's morning. Some employees also value flexibility and prefer to answer a quick message at night rather than stay late at the office.

These concerns suggest that the rule should be flexible rather than absolute. Organisations could agree clear policies, for example by allowing contact outside working hours only for urgent matters, and by compensating staff who are required to be on call. Email systems can also be set to deliver non-urgent messages the next morning.

In conclusion, although some exceptions are necessary, I believe employees should generally have the right to disconnect from work outside their working hours, because rest is essential for both their wellbeing and their performance.

speaking.cue:
Describe a time when you received some good news.
You should say:
- what the news was
- how you received it
- who you shared it with
and explain how you felt about it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about the day I found out I'd been accepted to my university. I'd taken the admission test about a month earlier, and I wasn't very confident, because the maths section had been really difficult. The results were supposed to be published online at ten in the morning, so I was sitting in front of my laptop at nine fifty, refreshing the page every few seconds. Of course, the website crashed because thousands of students were trying to access it at the same time. In the end, a friend messaged me a screenshot of the list, and I saw my name on it. At first I didn't believe it, so I checked my registration number three times. Then I ran into the kitchen to tell my mother, who was cooking, and she was so happy she started crying. My father was at work, so I called him, and he left the office early to buy sweets for the whole neighbourhood, which is a tradition in my family when there's good news. I felt an incredible sense of relief, because I'd been studying for that test for over a year. I also felt proud that all that hard work had paid off.
